rh-l2q4-d1e6458.summary: Alternatively, for both confirmation and obstinacy: the will's indifference is finite, so as a habit inclines it, a creatable habit can necessitate it. In the blessed this is confirmed grace, which with clear vision and the light of glory necessitates the will to love God in the manner of nature. In the bad, a habit of hatred and darkness of error with perverse judgment is inflicted as punishment and conserved by God, so they cannot act well. So Lombard says the damned's free will is depressed and corrupted, best understood as a created habit that fixes the will; they deserved it by sinning, and their consequent acts and habits are punishments, though perhaps not new demerits.
claims: The will's finite indifference can be necessitated by a habit.
Confirmed grace, vision, and light of glory necessitate the blessed.
A habit of hatred inflicted as punishment causes the obstinacy of demons.

rh-l2q4-d1e6530.summary: Second point: whether guardian angels merit and demons demerit. Neither side can reasonably be proved or disproved. Good angels perform many free virtuous acts in grace, which seems enough for merit; bad ones many free vicious acts, as Raphael could move faster or slower and demons could choose lesser or worse evils. So probably the good merit and the bad demerit.
claims: Whether angels merit or demerit cannot be proved either way.
Probably good angels merit and demons demerit.

rh-l2q4-d1e6583.summary: Many say they do not progress in beatific cognition or love but in other cognition, which does not pertain to beatitude, as Lombard says. Against: a blessed angel can do as good an act as a wayfarer, who thereby merits increase of essential reward, so the angel too.
claims: If wayfarers merit essential reward, angels would too.

rh-l2q4-d1e6603.summary: Easily answered by the first conclusion: strict merit is a free act conforming to a law that promises reward. God can command without promising reward, so 'the angel acts as well as a wayfarer, so merits equally' is not formal; God does not please to reward their acts, as enjoying God is a free virtuous act without further reward. Good angels act virtuously without hope of further merit, being sufficiently rewarded. Demons are cast out of God's household and released from his precept, so their deeds are not demeritorious, as a dog biting a saint does what in a man would be sin; God does not care to inflict new penalties for them.
claims: Merit requires a law promising reward.
Good angels act virtuously without meriting further essential reward.
Demons, released from precept, do not demerit.

rh-l2q4-d1e6681.summary: The Irishman says they sin but do not properly demerit eternal punishment, not being wayfarers, their acts damnatory rather than demeritorious; Scotus holds they demerit temporal punishment and so sin venially, not mortally, having no precept to avoid and not knowing God's good pleasure, only perhaps his counsel to the contrary. After judgment they will not sin at all, having no freedom.
claims: According to Scotus and the Irishman, demons sin venially, not mortally.

rh-l2q4-d1e6719.summary: A modern distinguishes sin as act, deformity, or guilt (reatus). Demons are continually in sin in the second and third senses; in the first they sin anew, willing men damned or sinning, against the precept of charity. Necessity does not excuse, since they caused it themselves, like the drunkard (Aristotle), and impotence from fault never excuses (Anselm). So they sin mortally anew until judgment, after which they will have no objects for new evil. Their pain of sense, accidental, increases until judgment, though not their pain of loss; they tempt men preferring lesser punishment now to delay the greater by delaying the number of the elect.
claims: According to a modern, demons sin mortally anew until judgment.
Self-caused necessity does not excuse.
Demons tempt to delay the judgment and their greater punishment.

rh-l2q4-d1e6841.summary: Against the first view: if they sin venially, either against a precept or not; if not, they do not sin; if so, there seems no reason their precept carries a lesser penalty than a wayfarer's.
claims: Venial sin of demons is incoherent.

rh-l2q4-d1e6861.summary: Further: if they know only God's counsel to the contrary, they do not sin at all, since acting against counsel is not sin, or everyone not following all counsels would sin venially.
claims: Acting against counsel is not sin.

rh-l2q4-d1e6880.summary: The second view seems very probable, except that it does not adequately explain why the damned will not demerit after judgment, saying they will lack objects for new evil works.
claims: The modern view is probable but its account of post-judgment sinlessness is inadequate.

rh-l2q4-d1e6898.summary: Against: every evil work is a work of will, and they will have objects for new bad volitions, since it is implausible they will never have bad volitions after judgment.
claims: The damned will still have objects for bad volitions.

rh-l2q4-d1e6914.summary: Further: willing evil for a year is worse than for a day, so the damned's malice will at least grow continually by the circumstance of time. No man can discern which of these is truer.
claims: The damned's malice grows by duration.
Human reason cannot settle these questions.

rh-l2q4-d1e6927.summary: Third point: replies to the arguments of the principal.

rh-l2q4-d1e6934.summary: To the first: in the good, freedom does not remain toward all acts, so they cannot sin, but toward some goods freedom of indifference remains, so they can merit at least accidental reward. In the bad, natural powers are intact, most splendid by nature (Dionysius), but depressed by vicious habits as to fault. God is direct cause of hardening by infusing the habit, but not first cause in every genus; the sinning creature is in a way prior, since God creates the habit because it deserved punishment. So Augustine's 'God is not the first cause of a creature's becoming worse' is true.
claims: The blessed retain freedom of indifference toward some goods.
God directly causes the hardening habit, but the sinner is the prior cause.

rh-l2q4-d1e6988.summary: To the second: the inference fails, since despite confirmation the good can merit accidental reward and the bad accidental punishment.
claims: Confirmation is compatible with merit of accidental reward.

rh-l2q4-d1e7001.summary: To the third: they know human damnation increases their misery, but less than it will after judgment, so they choose lesser punishment now to delay the greater.
claims: Demons choose present lesser misery to delay greater.

rh-l2q4-d1e7021.summary: Or: anger and envy give them erroneous judgments, so they prefer harming themselves and others to not harming others. They can will what increases their misery, though not precisely for that end. Anselm's argument concerns the angel before the fall, in the state he calls beatitude, which could not will what would make it miserable; the damned can.
claims: Envy gives demons erroneous judgments.
Anselm's principle applies to the unfallen angel, not to demons.

rh-l2q4-d1e7063.summary: To the fourth: ministering angels do no act to which they are bound by mere freedom of indifference, else they could omit it and sin; but they do some things not obligatory, by counsel or good will, whose omission would not be sin.
claims: Angels act freely only in non-obligatory acts.

rh-l2q4-d1e7096.summary: To the fifth: grants all, as said in the second point.
claims: Demons' ongoing sins may increase their punishment.

rh-l2q4-d1e7107.summary: To the sixth: the devil is obstinate and God does not co-act with him for any right or good act, so he can do nothing good. Even if he judged it good to have justice, he cannot conform to it justly with good circumstances; he can will to be just to escape punishment, but not will justice justly, his free will being depressed by the hardening habit and the withdrawal of divine cooperation (Lombard).
claims: The devil cannot will justice justly.
God does not co-act with the devil for good acts.

rh-l2q4-d1e7150.summary: Reply to the seventh principal argument: grants every man must discern when a good angel incites and when a bad one; one can have an act of discernment without the habit or gift, and should ask God for it when need and doubt arise.
claims: Everyone needs acts of discernment of spirits, which one should ask of God.

rh-l2q4-d1e7174.summary: Reply to the eighth: doctors commonly say vital operations are of two kinds: those like inanimate operations, consisting in local motion or collision of bodies (walking, speaking), and those unlike them (seeing, sensing). Angels seem to do the first but in truth only move bodies locally, causing sounds, so they do not properly walk or speak, these terms connoting a vital principle; the second they in no way do, neither sensing, seeing, nor generating.
claims: Angels in assumed bodies only move bodies locally.
Angels do not properly walk, speak, sense, or generate.

rh-l2q4-d1e7230.summary: Objection: incubus and succubus demons generate, as Josephus and Genesis 6 report giants born of angels and women, and Augustine (City of God XV) affirms from reliable witnesses. Reply: not by their own seed but by men's, the same demon acting as succubus to a man and incubus to a woman, so the child is the man's son. The same holds of angels' operations.
claims: Demonic generation uses human seed, so the child is human.

rh-l2q4-d1e7276.summary: Reply to the ninth: grants new thoughts in angels regarding knowledge by habits or species; Augustine means there are no changing thoughts concerning beatitude. A new thought of a charge does not remit thought of God, since God so co-acts with the beatific knowledge that it cannot be remitted, and the angel contemplates as distinctly as if thinking nothing else; among other thoughts, one intense thought may remit another.
claims: Beatific knowledge cannot be remitted by other thoughts.
Non-beatific angelic thoughts can change and compete.

rh-l2q4-d1e7320.summary: Reply to the tenth: Christ had no guardian angel, needing none, being a comprehensor in soul, and his humanity, united to God, could be neither impeded nor helped. The angel 'strengthened' him not by causing anything in him but by congratulating his fortitude, acting in the manner of one strengthening. This ends Holcot's last question on Book II.
claims: Christ had no guardian angel.
The angel's 'strengthening' of Christ was congratulation.

rh-l2q4-d1e7342.summary: Transitional rubric: there follows Holcot's single question on the third book of the Sentences.
